script.opening: "Hi. So I found this lump in my neck — here, at the front — and it bobs up and down when I swallow, which my friend who's a nurse said means it's thyroid. The thyroid blood test came back normal though, so I'm guessing it's nothing and I can just leave it? I don't really want a fuss over a lump that isn't even causing me any trouble. It's not painful or anything."

facts.text: If asked: found it about six weeks ago putting on a necklace. Front of the neck, slightly to the right, "about the size of a grape". Not painful. You think it might be a little bigger than when you first noticed it, but you are not sure. On video you can point to it and swallow — it moves up and down.
No change in your voice, no hoarseness, no difficulty swallowing, no choking, no noisy breathing or breathlessness. No other lumps you have felt in your neck.
No palpitations, tremor, weight change, heat or cold intolerance. Periods regular.

facts.topic: Past history — only if asked about past illnesses
facts.text: Hodgkin lymphoma at 15 — chemotherapy and radiotherapy to the neck and chest. "All clear for nearly 30 years." You stopped going to the late-effects follow-up clinic about 10 years ago.
Your aunt (mum's sister) had thyroid cancer in her 50s — "she had an operation and she's fine now".
44, accountant, married, two children aged 7 and 10. Never smoked. Drinks socially.

You are terrified of "cancer again". The lymphoma treatment was the worst year of your life and you swore you would never go through that again. That is why you want the normal blood test to be the answer. Say this only if asked about the lymphoma or what worries you.

Brisk and breezy — you want to be told to leave it. If the doctor accepts that, say thank you and go. If they explain that normal bloods do not rule out a problem and ask about your past, become quieter and admit the fear. You accept an urgent referral if it is explained as checking carefully, with the reassurance that most lumps are not cancer. Ask: "Will it be a big operation?" and "Do I have to tell the kids?"

ice.ideas: "It's thyroid, and the blood test was normal, so it's probably nothing."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): "I can't go through cancer again." Also the disruption to work and the children.
ice.expectations: "Can I just leave it?" You will accept a scan and referral if the reasons are explained calmly.

cues: "The blood test was normal though, so I'm guessing it's nothing." — say in the opening.
"I had treatment for lymphoma as a teenager — but that was ages ago." — say if asked about your medical history.
"I don't want to go through all that again." — say quietly if the lymphoma is explored.

checkpoints.text: Corrects the key misconception: a palpable thyroid nodule with NORMAL TFTs is NOT reassuring — most thyroid cancers are euthyroid — so normal bloods do not justify "leaving it"; a nodule needs examination, TSH and thyroid ULTRASOUND to risk-stratify
Elicits and weights the RISK FACTORS: previous head/neck irradiation (major) and family history of thyroid cancer, plus age — raising concern and the threshold to investigate/refer

Screens for RED FLAGS: rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule, hoarseness/voice change, dysphagia, cervical lymphadenopathy — and knows that under NICE NG12 an unexplained thyroid lump on its own meets the criterion to consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (her radiotherapy and family history make it clearly right), while stridor or breathing difficulty needs an immediate same-day opinion (British Thyroid Association 2014); tagged NICE NG12

Plans the correct work-up: examination (nodule characteristics + nodes), TSH (and thyroid antibodies if indicated), thyroid ULTRASOUND with risk-stratification (NICE NG230: an established grading system — in the UK usually BTA U1–U5; TIRADS systems are international alternatives), and FNA/specialist referral as indicated — in practice via the suspected cancer pathway given the NICE NG12 criterion and her risk factors — rather than reassurance from TFTs alone

Gives balanced information: most thyroid nodules are benign and many cancers are treatable with excellent outcomes — so investigation is precautionary, not a verdict — without either dismissing or catastrophising
Surfaces the cancer-survivor fear (the lymphoma history) gently and addresses it, rather than colluding with the "bloods are fine, leave it" avoidance
Handles the disruption/family worries and balances honesty with reassurance so she engages with assessment

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges the suspected cancer pathway referral (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days), advises reporting new hoarseness, rapid growth, swallowing difficulty (urgent) and any noisy breathing/stridor or breathing difficulty (same day — BTA 2014), confirms understanding/engagement, documents, and tracks the result

worked.txt: "I can see why a normal thyroid blood test feels reassuring — but here’s the important thing most people don’t know: a thyroid lump usually behaves with completely normal blood tests, even when it’s something we’d want to check. So ‘the bloods were fine’ doesn’t tell us about the lump itself. The way to assess a lump is to look at it directly with an ultrasound scan."

"Can I ask a couple of things? … You had radiotherapy to the neck as a teenager, for the lymphoma, and an aunt had thyroid cancer. Those both matter — they raise the importance of checking a thyroid lump properly. I’m not saying that to frighten you; I’m saying it’s exactly why we don’t just leave it."

"A few quick questions: has the lump grown quickly? Any change to your voice or hoarseness? Any trouble swallowing? Any other lumps in the neck? … Those help me judge how quickly to act. And I’ll feel the lump and your neck glands when I examine you."

"Two honest things together: the large majority of thyroid lumps turn out to be benign, and even the ones that aren’t are usually very treatable with good outcomes. AND, because of your history, we check properly rather than guess. Both are true — so this is precautionary, not me telling you it’s cancer."

"I suspect part of you has been hoping the normal bloods meant you could avoid all this — because you’ve been through cancer before and the thought of it coming back is terrifying. That fear makes complete sense. But having beaten it once, you of all people know that checking early is what gives the best outcome — not waiting."

"So: I’ll examine you and refer you on the fast-track route to the thyroid/neck-lump clinic — the NICE guidance, NICE NG12, supports that for a new thyroid lump, and your history makes it clearly right. They’ll do the ultrasound and, depending on what it shows, may take a tiny sample with a needle; the aim is an answer within 28 days. If meanwhile your voice changes, the lump grows fast, or you struggle to swallow, tell us straightaway — and any noisy breathing or difficulty breathing is same-day, A&E if we’re closed. I’ll follow the results through with you. You wanted to leave it; what I’m doing is making sure that if there’s anything to find, we find it early."

f.learning: A palpable thyroid nodule with NORMAL thyroid function is the rule, not reassurance — most thyroid cancers are euthyroid — so "the bloods were fine" must never justify leaving a nodule. The work-up is examination (nodule characteristics and cervical nodes), TSH, and thyroid ULTRASOUND with risk-stratification (U-classification/TIRADS) and FNA/specialist referral as indicated. Elicit and weight the risk factors — here previous head/neck irradiation (major) and family history of thyroid cancer — and screen the red flags (rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule, hoarseness/voice change, dysphagia, cervical lymphadenopathy). Under NICE NG12 an unexplained thyroid lump on its own meets the criterion to consider a suspected cancer pathway referral — her risk factors make it clearly right — and stridor needs an immediate same-day opinion (British Thyroid Association 2014). The examinable hidden agenda is cancer-survivor fear: treated for lymphoma as a teenager, she uses the normal TFTs as permission to avoid facing a possible new cancer. Surface and address that fear, balance honesty with reassurance (most nodules benign, thyroid cancer usually very treatable), and complete the ultrasound/referral with a clear safety-net for compressive/voice red flags.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG230 (2022) thyroid cancer · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · British Thyroid Association thyroid cancer guidelines (2014)
knowledge.summary: A new thyroid lump needs ultrasound assessment whatever the thyroid function. With past neck radiotherapy and a family history of thyroid cancer, refer on the suspected cancer pathway.

points.h: Normal TFTs settle nothing about the lump
points.t: Most thyroid nodules, including most thyroid cancers, occur with normal thyroid function. TSH tells you whether the nodule is overactive; it does not tell you whether it is benign. A low TSH points to a possible hyperfunctioning nodule (lower cancer risk); a normal TSH, as here, means the nodule is assessed by imaging.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (for an appointment within 2 weeks) for thyroid cancer in people with an unexplained thyroid lump. No red flag is needed to meet this criterion; red flags and risk factors make the referral clearly right.

Previous radiation to the head or neck (especially in childhood or adolescence), family history of thyroid cancer, extremes of age, male sex, and a nodule that is growing. Her teenage neck radiotherapy for lymphoma is a major risk factor; her aunt’s thyroid cancer adds to it.

Rapid growth, a hard or fixed lump, hoarseness or voice change, difficulty swallowing, enlarged neck nodes. Stridor or breathing difficulty with a thyroid mass needs same-day assessment (British Thyroid Association 2014).

NICE NG230 (2022): greyscale ultrasound graded with an established system (in the UK usually the British Thyroid Association U1–U5 score) is the first diagnostic test; ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology is offered when the grade meets the threshold, or considered if there is other clinical concern. This happens in the specialist thyroid or neck-lump clinic.

Most thyroid nodules are benign, and differentiated thyroid cancer generally has a very good outlook when treated. Present referral as a way to find out, not a verdict. The NHS Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days of referral.

dg.d: Open question first; let her describe the lump and her reasoning about the normal blood test before correcting anything.
Young family and work pressures; what her teenage cancer treatment meant to her; why “no fuss” matters to her.
In-person examination of the nodule and neck nodes; TSH already normal; thyroid ultrasound with U grading ± FNA through the specialist clinic.
Benign nodule or cyst versus thyroid cancer; overactive nodule excluded by normal TSH; lymphoma recurrence considered through node and systemic questions.
Asked about growth, voice change, dysphagia, breathing difficulty and other lumps; elicited neck radiotherapy and family history of thyroid cancer.
An unexplained thyroid nodule in a woman with major risk factors: needs urgent assessment, cause not yet known.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12) with ultrasound ± FNA; honest balance of likely benign and treatable; practical help with appointments.
Linked the radiotherapy history to her future care (late effects); offered support for the emotional impact of being a cancer survivor.
Examination booked; referral tracked; same-day contact for voice or swallowing change, 999 for breathing difficulty; ring if no appointment within a week.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the pause about the lymphoma and the insistence the bloods were “fine”, and explored the fear underneath.
Idea (normal bloods mean nothing is wrong); concern (a new cancer, and disruption to family and work); expectation (to be told to leave it).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath (only if asked): "I can't go through cancer again." Also the disruption to work and the children — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Priya, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for sending the photo. Before I say anything about it, tell me about the lump and what you’ve been thinking.
model.why: Starts with her account and her thinking

model.text: I found it at the front of my neck and it bobs up and down when I swallow. My friend’s a nurse and said that’s thyroid. The blood test came back normal, so I’m guessing I can just leave it? It’s not painful and it’s not bothering me.
That’s really clear, thank you. I’d like to ask a few questions, then explain what the normal blood test does and doesn’t tell us, and then we’ll agree what to do together. Is that all right?
model.why: Signposts the structure of the consultation

model.text: Sure. I don’t want a big fuss though.
I hear that. When did you first notice it, and has it changed since?
A little while ago. Not that I’ve noticed — it just seems to be there.
Any change in your voice, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or any difficulty breathing, especially lying flat?
model.why: Screens for compressive and nerve red flags

model.text: No, none of that.
Any other lumps in your neck, or feeling hot, shaky or losing weight?
No. I feel fine.
Good. A couple of background questions that matter for thyroid lumps. Have you ever had radiotherapy or any treatment to your head or neck?
model.why: Asks directly about the key risk factor

model.text: (pause) I had lymphoma as a teenager. I had radiotherapy to my neck. But that was years ago.
Thank you for telling me. And has anyone in your family had thyroid problems or thyroid cancer?
My aunt had thyroid cancer.
I noticed you went quiet when you mentioned the lymphoma. What’s it been like, finding a lump, after everything you went through then?
model.why: Picks up the non-verbal cue and opens the survivor fear

model.text: (quietly) Honestly? Terrifying. I keep telling myself it’s nothing because the bloods were normal. I can’t go through all that again — not with the kids and work.

That makes complete sense. You’ve been through cancer treatment before, so a lump brings all of that back. Hoping the blood test was the answer is a very human thing to do. What would help most from today?
model.why: Validates the avoidance and elicits expectations

model.text: I suppose… to know whether I really need to do anything.

Let me be straight with you. The blood test checks whether the thyroid is making the right amount of hormone. Most thyroid lumps — including the ones we want to check — come with a completely normal blood test. So it doesn’t tell us what the lump is. The way to look at a lump is an ultrasound scan.
model.why: Corrects the misconception that normal TFTs are reassuring

model.text: Oh. I really thought that was it.

Most people do. Two things are true at the same time. Most thyroid lumps are benign. And because you had neck radiotherapy and your aunt had thyroid cancer, the right thing is to check this one properly and quickly, not wait and watch.
model.why: Weights the risk factors while keeping perspective

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.

No — I don’t know what it is, and nobody can tell from a photo or a blood test. This is precautionary. If it did turn out to be a thyroid cancer, most are very treatable with a good outlook. And you know better than anyone that finding things early is what gives the best result.
model.why: Honest, balanced answer that uses her own experience

model.text: Here’s what I suggest. I’ll refer you to the specialist thyroid clinic on the urgent suspected-cancer pathway. They’ll scan the lump and, if the scan suggests it, take a tiny sample with a fine needle. The aim is an answer within about four weeks. I’d also like to examine your neck in person, ideally this week.
model.why: NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway, ultrasound ± FNA, in-person examination

model.text: Urgent? That sounds scary. And I’ve got the kids and work.
Urgent means quick, not that something bad has been found. It spares you weeks of wondering. What would make the appointments easier to manage?
model.why: Reframes urgency and problem-solves the practical barrier

model.text: If I know the dates early, I can sort cover.
Then I’ll ask the clinic to contact you directly, and our team will check the referral has gone through. I’ll give you a letter for work if you need one.
model.why: Practical support and a system to track the referral

model.text: While you wait: if your voice changes, the lump grows quickly, or you have trouble swallowing, contact us that day. Any difficulty breathing or noisy breathing is 999. If you haven’t heard from the clinic within a week, ring us. Can you tell me what you’ll do next?
model.why: Specific safety-net, referral tracking and teach-back

model.text: Come in for you to check my neck, wait for the thyroid clinic, and ring if I don’t hear in a week. Ring straight away if my voice or swallowing changes.
Exactly. You came hoping to leave it; I think you’re being brave by checking it instead. Is there anything else on your mind?
model.why: Acknowledges her feelings and invites anything unsaid

model.text: No. Thanks — I think I needed someone to say it.

social.t: Young children and a job make appointments hard. Offering early dates, a work letter and help with planning makes attendance more likely.
Survivors of childhood or teenage cancer often carry fear of recurrence. Avoidance (“the bloods were fine”) is a common, understandable response; naming it gently helps.

legal.t: She has capacity and may decline referral. If she does, the GP’s duty is to make sure the decision is informed — explain the risk clearly, record it, and leave the door open (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Practices should track suspected cancer referrals so that a missed or delayed appointment is noticed. Tell her what to do if she hears nothing.
A photo is not an examination. Arrange a face-to-face examination of the nodule and neck nodes rather than deciding on video alone.

community.t: The British Thyroid Foundation for information about thyroid nodules; Macmillan Cancer Support if a cancer is diagnosed, and for survivorship worries.

redFlags: Rapid growth, a hard or fixed lump, or enlarged neck nodes
Hoarseness or voice change, difficulty swallowing
Stridor or difficulty breathing — same-day assessment
Risk factors: neck radiotherapy in adolescence; aunt with thyroid cancer
psychosocial: Teenage lymphoma and its treatment — what that experience means now
Young family and work; fear of disruption
Using the normal blood test as a reason not to look further
ice: Idea: “The thyroid blood test was normal, so the lump is nothing”
Concern: a new cancer, and not wanting to go through treatment again
Expectation: to be told she can leave it

playbook.diagnosis: An unexplained thyroid nodule (about 2.5 cm) in a euthyroid woman with previous neck radiotherapy and a family history of thyroid cancer. Normal TFTs do not help decide its nature; it needs ultrasound grading ± FNA on the suspected cancer pathway.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The blood test is like checking a factory’s output — it’s making the right amount. It doesn’t tell us about a lump on the building. To look at the lump itself, we use an ultrasound scan.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping the normal blood test meant you could leave this, and after what you went through as a teenager, I completely understand why. Checking it quickly is the way to stop it hanging over you.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the survivor fear; frame the referral as finding out, not a diagnosis; help with the practical side (early dates, a work letter).
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the thyroid or neck-lump clinic (NICE NG12)
Ultrasound with U grading and FNA if indicated (NICE NG230)
Face-to-face examination of the nodule and neck nodes
safetyNet: Voice change, rapid growth or trouble swallowing — contact the practice the same day; breathing difficulty — 999
Ring if no clinic appointment within a week; review once results are back

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient. The normal thyroid test sounds reassuring, the patient wants to leave it, and the two risk factors only come out if you ask. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Accepting “the bloods were normal” as reassurance and agreeing to watch the lump.
items.why: Most thyroid cancers occur with normal TFTs. NICE NG12 says consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for any unexplained thyroid lump.
items.fix: Explain what the blood test measures and doesn’t, then refer for ultrasound assessment.

items.fail: Never asking about radiotherapy or family history.
items.why: She doesn’t connect her teenage treatment to the lump. Missing it loses the key risk factor that should firm up the referral.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Have you ever had radiotherapy to your head or neck? Anyone in the family with thyroid cancer?”

items.fail: Deciding everything from the photo on a video call.
items.why: A photo can’t tell you if a lump is hard, fixed, or has nodes around it.
items.fix: Arrange a face-to-face neck examination alongside the referral; don’t delay the referral for it.

items.fail: Moving straight past the pause after “I had lymphoma”.
items.why: The survivor fear is the hidden agenda; if it isn’t named, her avoidance wins and she may not attend.
items.fix: “You went quiet when you mentioned the lymphoma. What’s it like finding a lump after that?”

items.fail: Swinging from reassurance to alarm: “With your history this could well be cancer.”
items.why: Unbalanced alarm frightens a survivor into further avoidance and is not accurate — most nodules are benign.
items.fix: Say both: most thyroid lumps are benign, and her history is why we check quickly.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will be in touch” and no plan if they aren’t.
items.why: Vague safety-netting and untracked referrals are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the red flags, say what to do if she hears nothing in a week, and check understanding with teach-back.

timeMap.d: She opens with “the bloods were normal, can I leave it?”. Hear her reasoning before correcting it.
Onset and growth, voice, swallowing, breathing, other lumps. Ask directly about head or neck radiotherapy and family history — she won’t volunteer either.
Follow the pause after “lymphoma”. Name the survivor fear and the worry about family and work.
Normal TFTs don’t assess a lump; ultrasound does. Most nodules are benign, but her risk factors mean the suspected cancer pathway. Examine in person.
Voice, swallowing, rapid growth — same day; breathing difficulty — 999. Ring if no appointment in a week. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees the normal thyroid test means the lump can be left; never asks about radiotherapy or family history; or announces “this could be cancer” without balance and moves on; no referral, no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Explains that normal TFTs don’t assess a nodule; elicits the radiotherapy and family history; asks the red-flag questions; refers on the suspected cancer pathway for ultrasound ± FNA; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: follows the cue about the lymphoma and names the survivor fear kindly; balances “most are benign” with “your history means we check”; turns her experience into a reason to act; solves the childcare and work barrier; tracks the referral and checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Your thyroid test is normal, so that’s reassuring.”
avoid.instead: “The blood test tells us how the thyroid is working, not what the lump is. The scan tells us about the lump.”
avoid.why: Normal TFTs are the rule with thyroid cancer; this sentence is the clinical trap of the station.

avoid.dont: “With your history, we need to rule out cancer urgently.”
avoid.instead: “Most thyroid lumps are benign. Because of your neck radiotherapy, we check this one quickly rather than wait.”
avoid.why: Leading with cancer, unbalanced, confirms her worst fear and can drive further avoidance.

avoid.dont: “Let’s just keep an eye on it and recheck your bloods in a few months.”
avoid.instead: “I’d like a scan through the specialist thyroid clinic, and I’ll refer you today.”
avoid.why: Watchful waiting with repeat TFTs fails the NICE NG12 criterion and her risk profile.

SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes urgency and problem-solves the practical barrier

SCA_MODELS.text: If I know the dates early, I can sort cover.
Then I’ll ask the clinic to contact you directly, and our team will check the referral has gone through. I’ll give you a letter for work if you need one.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical support and a system to track the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: While you wait: if your voice changes, the lump grows quickly, or you have trouble swallowing, contact us that day. Any difficulty breathing or noisy breathing is 999. If you haven’t heard from the clinic within a week, ring us. Can you tell me what you’ll do next?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net, referral tracking and teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Come in for you to check my neck, wait for the thyroid clinic, and ring if I don’t hear in a week. Ring straight away if my voice or swallowing changes.
Exactly. You came hoping to leave it; I think you’re being brave by checking it instead. Is there anything else on your mind?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges her feelings and invites anything unsaid

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thanks — I think I needed someone to say it.

SCA_STEM.name: Priya Anand
pmh: Lymphoma in adolescence, treated — including radiotherapy to the neck
SCA_STEM.recent: Self-found lump at the front of the neck. Thyroid function tests (practice nurse) normal. Photo sent before the call: a single swelling in the thyroid area, estimated at about 2.5 cm.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss the neck lump and her normal thyroid blood test.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG230 (2022) thyroid cancer · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · British Thyroid Association thyroid cancer guidelines (2014)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A new thyroid lump needs ultrasound assessment whatever the thyroid function. With past neck radiotherapy and a family history of thyroid cancer, refer on the suspected cancer pathway.

points.h: Normal TFTs settle nothing about the lump
points.t: Most thyroid nodules, including most thyroid cancers, occur with normal thyroid function. TSH tells you whether the nodule is overactive; it does not tell you whether it is benign. A low TSH points to a possible hyperfunctioning nodule (lower cancer risk); a normal TSH, as here, means the nodule is assessed by imaging.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (for an appointment within 2 weeks) for thyroid cancer in people with an unexplained thyroid lump. No red flag is needed to meet this criterion; red flags and risk factors make the referral clearly right.

Previous radiation to the head or neck (especially in childhood or adolescence), family history of thyroid cancer, extremes of age, male sex, and a nodule that is growing. Her teenage neck radiotherapy for lymphoma is a major risk factor; her aunt’s thyroid cancer adds to it.

Rapid growth, a hard or fixed lump, hoarseness or voice change, difficulty swallowing, enlarged neck nodes. Stridor or breathing difficulty with a thyroid mass needs same-day assessment (British Thyroid Association 2014).

NICE NG230 (2022): greyscale ultrasound graded with an established system (in the UK usually the British Thyroid Association U1–U5 score) is the first diagnostic test; ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology is offered when the grade meets the threshold, or considered if there is other clinical concern. This happens in the specialist thyroid or neck-lump clinic.

Most thyroid nodules are benign, and differentiated thyroid cancer generally has a very good outlook when treated. Present referral as a way to find out, not a verdict. The NHS Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days of referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her describe the lump and her reasoning about the normal blood test before correcting anything.
Young family and work pressures; what her teenage cancer treatment meant to her; why “no fuss” matters to her.
Picked up the pause about the lymphoma and the insistence the bloods were “fine”, and explored the fear underneath.
Idea (normal bloods mean nothing is wrong); concern (a new cancer, and disruption to family and work); expectation (to be told to leave it).
In-person examination of the nodule and neck nodes; TSH already normal; thyroid ultrasound with U grading ± FNA through the specialist clinic.
Benign nodule or cyst versus thyroid cancer; overactive nodule excluded by normal TSH; lymphoma recurrence considered through node and systemic questions.
Asked about growth, voice change, dysphagia, breathing difficulty and other lumps; elicited neck radiotherapy and family history of thyroid cancer.
An unexplained thyroid nodule in a woman with major risk factors: needs urgent assessment, cause not yet known.
Suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12) with ultrasound ± FNA; honest balance of likely benign and treatable; practical help with appointments.
Linked the radiotherapy history to her future care (late effects); offered support for the emotional impact of being a cancer survivor.
Examination booked; referral tracked; same-day contact for voice or swallowing change, 999 for breathing difficulty; ring if no appointment within a week.

social.t: Young children and a job make appointments hard. Offering early dates, a work letter and help with planning makes attendance more likely.
Survivors of childhood or teenage cancer often carry fear of recurrence. Avoidance (“the bloods were fine”) is a common, understandable response; naming it gently helps.

legal.t: She has capacity and may decline referral. If she does, the GP’s duty is to make sure the decision is informed — explain the risk clearly, record it, and leave the door open (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Practices should track suspected cancer referrals so that a missed or delayed appointment is noticed. Tell her what to do if she hears nothing.
A photo is not an examination. Arrange a face-to-face examination of the nodule and neck nodes rather than deciding on video alone.

community.t: The British Thyroid Foundation for information about thyroid nodules; Macmillan Cancer Support if a cancer is diagnosed, and for survivorship worries.

redFlags: Rapid growth, a hard or fixed lump, or enlarged neck nodes
Hoarseness or voice change, difficulty swallowing
Stridor or difficulty breathing — same-day assessment
Risk factors: neck radiotherapy in adolescence; aunt with thyroid cancer
psychosocial: Teenage lymphoma and its treatment — what that experience means now
Young family and work; fear of disruption
Using the normal blood test as a reason not to look further
ice: Idea: “The thyroid blood test was normal, so the lump is nothing”
Concern: a new cancer, and not wanting to go through treatment again
Expectation: to be told she can leave it

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: An unexplained thyroid nodule (about 2.5 cm) in a euthyroid woman with previous neck radiotherapy and a family history of thyroid cancer. Normal TFTs do not help decide its nature; it needs ultrasound grading ± FNA on the suspected cancer pathway.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The blood test is like checking a factory’s output — it’s making the right amount. It doesn’t tell us about a lump on the building. To look at the lump itself, we use an ultrasound scan.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping the normal blood test meant you could leave this, and after what you went through as a teenager, I completely understand why. Checking it quickly is the way to stop it hanging over you.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the survivor fear; frame the referral as finding out, not a diagnosis; help with the practical side (early dates, a work letter).
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the thyroid or neck-lump clinic (NICE NG12)
Ultrasound with U grading and FNA if indicated (NICE NG230)
Face-to-face examination of the nodule and neck nodes
safetyNet: Voice change, rapid growth or trouble swallowing — contact the practice the same day; breathing difficulty — 999
Ring if no clinic appointment within a week; review once results are back

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient. The normal thyroid test sounds reassuring, the patient wants to leave it, and the two risk factors only come out if you ask. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Accepting “the bloods were normal” as reassurance and agreeing to watch the lump.
items.why: Most thyroid cancers occur with normal TFTs. NICE NG12 says consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for any unexplained thyroid lump.
items.fix: Explain what the blood test measures and doesn’t, then refer for ultrasound assessment.

items.fail: Never asking about radiotherapy or family history.
items.why: She doesn’t connect her teenage treatment to the lump. Missing it loses the key risk factor that should firm up the referral.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Have you ever had radiotherapy to your head or neck? Anyone in the family with thyroid cancer?”

items.fail: Deciding everything from the photo on a video call.
items.why: A photo can’t tell you if a lump is hard, fixed, or has nodes around it.
items.fix: Arrange a face-to-face neck examination alongside the referral; don’t delay the referral for it.

items.fail: Moving straight past the pause after “I had lymphoma”.
items.why: The survivor fear is the hidden agenda; if it isn’t named, her avoidance wins and she may not attend.
items.fix: “You went quiet when you mentioned the lymphoma. What’s it like finding a lump after that?”

items.fail: Swinging from reassurance to alarm: “With your history this could well be cancer.”
items.why: Unbalanced alarm frightens a survivor into further avoidance and is not accurate — most nodules are benign.
items.fix: Say both: most thyroid lumps are benign, and her history is why we check quickly.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will be in touch” and no plan if they aren’t.
items.why: Vague safety-netting and untracked referrals are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the red flags, say what to do if she hears nothing in a week, and check understanding with teach-back.
